Purpose: A short, friendly walkthrough that explains how Claude, MCP, and skills fit together — the fastest way to get oriented if you're brand new.
When to Use: Say things like “I'm new here,” “onboard me,” or “explain how this works” — or just ask when you're confused about MCP or skills.
Where to Use: Anywhere, for anyone starting out — developers, PMs, designers, support, sales, or data roles.
How to Use: Type /start, or just say you're new — Claude will pick it up automatically. (See the install guide below: this skill needs to be saved to the right folder first before it will actually run.)
Input Requirements: Just answer two quick questions: your role, and whether you've used AI tools like this before. Nothing else needed.
Expected Output: A short interactive lesson, right in the chat. If you want, it can also save you a one-page cheat sheet and a completion summary — but only after you say yes.
Notes: Only ever writes files after you explicitly say okay, and only inside the output/onboarding/ folder — it won't touch anything else.

Purpose: A deeper, more thorough version of onboarding for people who are completely new to Claude Code or non-technical — it doesn't finish until you can work on your own.
When to Use: Say things like “I am new here,” “this is my first task,” or “I don't understand MCP” — use this one if Start feels too quick.
Where to Use: Formal onboarding for a new employee, especially before their first real task.
How to Use: Type /new-joinee, optionally followed by your role or first task (e.g. /new-joinee support agent). (See the install guide below: needs to be saved to the right folder first.)
Input Requirements: Your name, role, first assigned task, and whether you've used tools like this before. You'll also be asked to say yes before anything gets saved.
Expected Output: A full teaching session that ends with two short checks. Pass both and you also get a completion certificate — everything saved under onboarding-output/.
Notes: Heads up: as written, this skill can currently only read files, not write them — but it's designed to save your cheat sheet and certificate. That mismatch needs sorting out before those files can actually appear.

Purpose: Helps you create a brand-new Claude skill from scratch, or review and improve one that already exists.
When to Use: Whenever you want to build a new skill, clean up an existing one, or aren't sure if a skill is set up well.
Where to Use: Anywhere skills are being written or maintained for this project.
How to Use: Type /skill-builder, or just say you want to create or improve a skill. It asks a short series of questions first before writing anything. (See the install guide below.)
Input Requirements: Answers to a short back-and-forth: what the skill should do, what triggers it, and what it should never do. Skips questions you've already answered up front.
Expected Output: A new or improved skill file, following the project's standard quality checklist.
Notes: One thing to know: it links out to a file called reference.md, but in this repository that file is actually named reference_skill_builder.md, so the link doesn't resolve as written.

Purpose: Gives you a guided, read-only tour of an unfamiliar project — what it's for, how it's organized, and what's safe to try first.
When to Use: Ask for a tour, ask Claude to explain what's in a project, or say you want to understand a codebase before touching it.
Where to Use: The very start of working in any project you haven't seen before.
How to Use: Type /project-discovery, optionally with a folder path. (See the install guide below.)
Input Requirements: Nothing required — just point it at a project, or let it use the current one.
Expected Output: A plain-language summary in chat: what the project does, its folders, what skills exist, what's connected, and one safe first step. It never creates any files.
Notes: One inconsistency worth flagging: its settings technically allow it to run any terminal command, but its own instructions say to only run three specific, harmless git commands — worth confirming which one actually applies.

Purpose: Checks whether something similar already exists before you build it from scratch — saves you from accidentally duplicating work.
When to Use: Before creating any new file, report, script, dashboard, or skill — or any time you're not sure if this already exists somewhere.
Where to Use: Anywhere in this project, right before starting new work.
How to Use: Type /existing-asset-finder followed by a short description of what you're about to build. (See the install guide below.)
Input Requirements: A short description of the thing you're thinking of building — a name, a purpose, or even a rough idea is enough to start.
Expected Output: A short report recommending REUSE, EXTEND, MERGE, CREATE, or STOP, with the evidence behind that call.
Notes: It only looks, never touches anything — it won't create, change, or delete a single file, even if it recommends doing so. Acting on it is always up to you.

Purpose: Turns a fuzzy, half-formed task (“I need to do X but I'm not sure how”) into a clear, honest plan — showing exactly what's confirmed and what's still a guess.
When to Use: Whenever a request feels vague or you're not sure where to start — especially useful for your first few tasks in a new role.
Where to Use: Right at the start of any unclear task, before you dive in.
How to Use: Type /first-task-mapper followed by your task, or just describe it and answer the follow-up questions. (See the install guide below.)
Input Requirements: A description of the task, then a short back-and-forth: the actual goal, where the data comes from, who reviews the result, and so on.
Expected Output: A clear one-page plan in chat, with every detail labelled Confirmed, Assumption, or Unknown, plus a readiness verdict. Saves to a file only if you ask.
Notes: Important: it only plans the work, it never does the task itself — and it won't guess at things like who should review the result; it marks those “not confirmed” instead.

Purpose: Reviews a set of requirements or a project brief and flags anything missing, unclear, or contradictory before work starts on it.
When to Use: Before development begins on a document, ticket, or brief that feels incomplete or ambiguous.
Where to Use: Any pre-development review of requirements or acceptance criteria.
How to Use: Type /requirements-validator followed by a file path, or paste the requirements directly. (See the install guide below.)
Input Requirements: The requirements themselves — a file, a ticket, or pasted text. Background like business goals is optional but helpful.
Expected Output: A clear review in chat: what's missing, what's ambiguous, improved acceptance criteria, and any open questions still needing an answer.
Notes: Sticks strictly to what's actually written — it won't invent a requirement that isn't there, and won't rewrite your whole document unless that's genuinely needed for clarity.

Purpose: Cleans up messy Markdown formatting — inconsistent headings, mismatched bullet styles, broken tables — without changing a word of your actual content.
When to Use: Whenever a Markdown file looks messy or inconsistent and needs polishing before it's shared.
Where to Use: Any Markdown document that needs a formatting pass before review or publishing.
How to Use: Type /markdown-document-formatter followed by a file path, or paste the raw Markdown directly. (See the install guide below.)
Input Requirements: A Markdown file path, or the raw Markdown text pasted in.
Expected Output: A cleaned-up copy saved next to the original, named [original-name]-formatted.md, plus a short summary of exactly what was fixed.
Notes: Only fixes formatting and structure — never touches your original file, and never rewrites, shortens, or reworks your actual wording.

Purpose: Turns rough meeting notes into a clean, structured summary — attendees, decisions, action items with owners, and anything still unresolved.
When to Use: Right after a meeting, whenever you need notes turned into something shareable.
Where to Use: Any post-meeting follow-up or decision tracking.
How to Use: Type /meeting-note-summariser followed by a topic or date, then paste in your notes (or give a file path). (See the install guide below.)
Input Requirements: Your raw meeting notes, pasted in or as a file — a title or date is optional.
Expected Output: A tidy summary shown right in chat by default. It only saves a file if you specifically ask it to.
Notes: Never invents an attendee, decision, or deadline that wasn't actually in your notes — anything unclear is labelled “TBD” instead of guessed at.

Purpose: Drafts a polite, on-brand reply to a customer email — about an order, a refund, a delivery issue, or a general question — for you to review before sending.
When to Use: Whenever a customer email needs a reply drafted for you to check over.
Where to Use: Customer support conversations, before a human sends the final reply.
How to Use: Type /customer-email-reply-drafter and paste in the customer's email. (See the install guide below.)
Input Requirements: The customer's email content — a name, order number, or issue type helps but isn't required.
Expected Output: A ready-to-review draft reply in plain text, with clear placeholders (like [insert tracking number]) anywhere information is missing.
Notes: Never invents order or refund details it doesn't have, and never sends the email itself — sending is always a human decision.

Purpose: Turns a product name and a list of features into a polished, ready-to-publish product description.
When to Use: Whenever a new product listing needs description copy written.
Where to Use: E-commerce content prep, before a listing goes live.
How to Use: Type /product-description-writer followed by the product name, then give it the feature list. (See the install guide below.)
Input Requirements: The product name plus its features or specs, as a list. A preferred tone or target length is optional.
Expected Output: A polished title (if needed) and a finished description, in plain text or simple Markdown, ready to paste straight into a listing.
Notes: Uses Digitweb Lanka's standard tone — clear, benefit-led, UK English — and never makes up a product detail it wasn't given.

Purpose: Reads an orders CSV and gives you the headline numbers: total orders, total revenue, and your top 3 best-selling products.
When to Use: Whenever you need a quick revenue and top-seller snapshot from an orders export.
Where to Use: Basic order and revenue reporting for e-commerce.
How to Use: Type /order-summary-report followed by the path to your CSV. (See the install guide below.)
Input Requirements: An orders CSV with an order ID, an order total, and a product name or item column.
Expected Output: A plain-text summary: total orders, total revenue, and your top 3 products by quantity — plus a note on any rows it had to skip and why.
Notes: Read-only — never edits your CSV, and never makes up a number it can't actually calculate from the data.

Purpose: Reads an orders CSV and sorts every order into a clear status bucket — delivered, cancelled, on time, or delayed — so you can spot problems fast.
When to Use: Whenever you need to check delivery status across a batch of orders, especially to catch delays.
How to Use: Type /order-status-summary followed by the path to your CSV. (See the install guide below.)
Input Requirements: An orders CSV with order ID, customer name, order date, ship date, expected delivery date, and status columns.
Expected Output: Counts for each status bucket, plus a table of delayed orders sorted worst-first, so the most overdue ones are easy to spot.
Notes: If a required column is missing, it stops and asks you to fix the file rather than guessing at the answer.
